The political climate has significantly shifted since those days, so progressivism has become the new hipness for devlopers and publishers.

As to why the progressive ideology is so dominant in the industry, there's a few reasons. Firstly, from a developer side, there's immense pressure for people to be progressive. One of the biggest factors in acquiring game dev employment is who you know. Politically, devs have a status quo. Thirdly, on the subject of progressivism in games, going back to the changing political climate, it's worth noting that if you openly go anti-progressive as a dev or publisher, you'll receive a massive load of negative PR from entities with wide reaches. As for the rest of your grievances,

Game simplicity/dumbing down is a result of a shifting audience. Thanks to the casual boom of the mid-2000s, sowed by those such as Wii-era Nintendo and Zynga, devs and publishers realized that casuals are a pretty massive audience. As such, they have to be factored into the game development process, particularly in AAA games, which are designed to appeal to broad audiences. And because of the preferences of casual players, games have been dumbed down for their sake as a result.

Unfinished games are the result of the "We-can-fix-it-later" mindset thanks to patches. For most of the history of games, what you got out of the box was what you got period, so there had to be more stringent QA in order to prevent post-release disasters. Nowadays, devs/publishers can release half-finished games under the premise that they'll fix the holes later on. Releasing games in such a state allows them to get out into the market faster, thus bringing in money quicker. Early Access is also a big factor in this mindset, for basically the same reasons.

As for mobile games, this is another demographic issue. Phone games have been shown to rake in massive amounts of money, so the game industry is just following that money. The presence of smartphones on a global stage has also been on the increase, while other mediums have been relatively stagnant.

As for always-online, it's more a DRM thing than anything else, although consumers allowing it has helped establish it. Increased Internet access has also been a factor.

As for price, I'd say calling modern games "More expensive" is a half-truth. Factoring in inflation, consoles and games have generally been going down in price the past few decades. They're only more expensive if you include microtransactions and DLC, which, to be fair, are increasingly common practice, even in "complete" games.

So long story short, games, as a medium, are being "destroyed" due to a combination of shifting demographics, social pressure, and gamers simply enabling it, causing devs to make games in a way that deviates from your (and, frankly my) ideals.
